Millions Missing

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Twenty to 30-million people worldwide have dropped out of life due to a mysterious illness that can't be cured, nor its origins traced. But is there finally hope after years of misdiagnosis?

Unique Selling Point:
Millions of very ill people are wrestling their lives back from misunderstanding and stigmatization around a crippling disease called myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) or chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS).

There’s no known cure for CFS and the origins are still poorly understood – to make matters worse, bad science that led to totally inappropriate understanding and treatment of the disease in the last five years very nearly became a prolonged death sentence for the millions of people living with CFS.



Summary:
CFS has been called a malingerer’s disease - it occurs in people of all ages, socio-economic levels and ethnic backgrounds, even toddlers as young as 2. Many doctors remain unconvinced of CFS as a genuine illness; no cause or diagnostic test exist.

Much damage was done to the CFS cause when in 2011 British researchers announced a major breakthrough in the highly respected journal Lancet. The researchers reported that ‘PACE’, the largest treatment trial ever had been a great success and "found" that the best way of dealing with CFS was exercise and psychotherapy. Graded exercise therapy (GET) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) would improve the symptoms and could even cure CFS. CBT would challenge patients’ beliefs that they have a physiological illness limiting their ability to exercise and so they need only to become more active and ignore their symptoms to fully recover.

Headlines around the world shouted, “Got ME? Just get out and exercise, say scientists.” The medical profession, including American CDC, soon set PACE as baseline for treatment guidelines.

Problem is, PACE was bad science. CFS sufferers realised it straight away. Science is only now catching up with exactly how bad. PACE contradicted patients' everyday experience that even mild exertion could increase all other symptoms and cause fatigue so profound that they could barely lift the sheets on their beds. It caused cognitive deficits, blood pressure problems, unrestorative sleep, neurological and immune dysfunction, among about 60 symptoms.

At first, the "Missing Millions" had no way of challenging the science, because the data of the study hadn’t been released, but what they COULD do was send emails, chat online…and form a community that began to fight back against their physical and conceptual imprisonment. A five-year battle ensued to review the actual data underlying the $8-million PACE study.


Further information:
In the last two months, in September, the Missing Millions made a great breakthrough when a British court ordered the PACE trial's original data to be released.

Rewind a few years - in South Africa, Retha Viviers had founded a Facebook support group that is growing at a steady pace and it encouraged her to begin the ME/CFS Foundation South Africa to focus on awareness, diagnosis, and treatment of the disease. Retha hooked up with the US-based Open Medicine Foundation of Dr Ronald Davis to bring home messages of hope; get financial support for bed-ridden breadwinners who have lost everything…and this Retha has done mostly from her own bed, as CFS forces her to economise every movement of her life.

In stark contrast to a silent, isolated world before social media, CFS patients were now able to start identifying patterns and shared experiences. They began to realise it’s not all in their heads and that most of them really do have to REST the minute they feel tired, not exercise...otherwise the next day they’d be semi-paralyzed, barely able to walk.

Many patients worked to bring the flaws of the PACE study to light. They wrote blogs, contacted the press, submitted carefully argued letters and commentaries to leading medical journals. They even published papers in peer-reviewed scientific journals.

Patients organised to file Freedom of Information Act requests to gain access to the trial data from Queen Mary University of London where the lead researcher worked.

The university denied most of the requests, saying they were “vexatious.” The study’s defenders painted critics as unhinged crusaders who were “impeding progress for the estimated 30-million ME/CFS patients around the world”.

Richard Horton, the editor of the Lancet described the trial’s critics as “a fairly small but highly organised, very vocal and very damaging group of individuals who have, I would say, actually hijacked this agenda and distorted the debate so that it actually harms the overwhelming majority of patients.”

Press reports alleged that ME/CFS researchers had received death threats, and they lumped the PACE critics in with the purported crazies.

But the online community of “activists” managed under court order to compel the British researchers to release their raw data which they did this past September.

PACE had seemed like a great study — big, controlled, peer-reviewed — but patients couldn’t reconcile the results with their own experience so as the dug into the data the saw enormous problems became clear and once they’d done their analyses, the investigation was taken forward by Dr. David Tuller, a lecturer in public health and journalism at UC Berkeley.

The collective effort helped demolish the credibility of the PACE trial as a piece of scientific research.

In February this year Virology Blog posted an open letter to The Lancet and its editor, Richard Horton, stating that the trial’s flaws “have no place in published research.” Surprisingly, the PACE authors, The Lancet, and others in the U.K. medical and academic establishment have continued their vigorous defense of the study, despite its glaring methodological and ethical deficiencies.

The analysis shows that if you’re already getting standard medical care, your chances of being helped by exercise and psychotherapy are at best 10% and chances of recovery nearly 0%.

Under the guidance of world-renowned geneticist Ronald W. Davis, PhD, Open Medicine Foundation has brought in top experts from a variety of fields for a bold and new collaborative research project with the ultimate goal of unlocking the mystery ME/CFS.
Davis’ own son, the 30-year old Whitney, suffers from CFS and Davis is determined to find a cure – even if it might be too late for his own son, who is reportedly terminally ill.

Davis' "End ME/CFS Project" was founded on the idea that a comprehensive, interdisciplinary effort is needed to produce breakthroughs in the understanding of ME/CFS and related chronic complex diseases (sometimes referred to as neuro-immune diseases). Their goal is to connect the best experts, from both inside and outside the field, through openness and information sharing.

Linda Tannenbaum, Open Medicine Foundation’s CEO/President also has a personal motivation for wanting to find answers as quickly as possible, because has a daughter suffering from ME/CFS.

The project’s first study is the ME/CFS Severely ill Big Data Study that is designed to find a clinically useful diagnostic biomarker.

“Almost all scientists do things that are easy,” said Dr. Davis. “That’s why no one has done this study before.”

Davis calls the PACE research a “classic bad study” that used such a broad definition of the disease that it likely included many patients who didn’t truly have ME/CFS at all.

Davis says the PACE study has to be retracted or even used as a teaching tool to have medical students identify how many things are wrong the study.

Retractions are rare, however, and erasing the impact of this flawed research will take much work for years to come.

Davis expects his project to succeed because it’s modeled after two former success stories – the The Human Genome Project, launched by James D. Watson, PhD, who is on our ME/CFS Scientific Advisory Board and the Consortium on Inflammation and Host Response to Injury in Humans, led by Ronald G. Tompkins, also on the ME/CFS Scientific Advisory Board.

For the first time, high level scientists are working on increasing understanding of the disease at a molecular level and find diagnostic markers, effective treatments, and a cure. They also hope to fine effective prevention strategies.

Press Release:


Missing Millions
It’s a mysterious illness that is notoriously difficult to diagnose and even describe. It causes debilitating fatigue and makes normal everyday activities such as getting out of bed, an impossible task. Affecting millions of people worldwide and after years of research, doctors are finally closer to finding a cause for this crippling disease. Carte Blanche looks into Chronic Fatigue – also known as Myalgic Encephalomyelitis.



PROMOS:
15”
How close is the breakthrough? We meet the scientists in a race against time to find a cure for crippling chronic fatigue syndrome.
RETHA VIVIERS: ...never before has there been so much hope...they have done more in one year than the past 30 years.

15”
NATHALIE WILLIAMS: They spend more money in the States on researching male pattern baldness than they do on ME and this is a disease that can be fatal.
Chronic Fatigue Syndrome patients stands up to demand better research -- but will the cure come in time?

10”
Lives lost to crippling chronic fatigue syndrome fight for research and recognition -- how long before science reveals the solutions that up to 20-million people are desperate for?


Script:


SCRIPT: MILLIONS MISSING
TX: 12 February 2017
PRODUCER: Anna-Maria van Niekerk

INSERT SCRIPT
NATHALIE WILLIAMS: I wake up every day of the life and it doesn’t matter how many hours I have slept. I still feel tired.
In Fourways Johannesburg, Nathalie Williams has moved back into her mom’s home. She’d love nothing better than to get out and go to work. Or take her dogs for a walk. But in the 26th year of living with myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome, she can’t.
NATHALIE WILLIAMS: I hate the term chronic fatigue syndrome...first of all, fatigue is...that doesn’t even come close to describing what it is and second of all, it’s...it’s a minor symptom really compared to the other stuff.
Nathalie would pay a high price for pushing through with this hour-long interview – they call it the push-crash cycle – crippling pain, debilitating brain fog – in ME it’s called post-exertional malaise. Like the worst influenza, it kicks in after a day or so – for some triggered by lifting the sheets on their bed – for Nathalie, being upright.
NATHALIE WILLIAMS: Anytime you’re upright, your heart has to pump more blood around the body and with people with ME, our hearts don’t pump blood properly...I start to sweat, I feel dizzy and I feel nauseous, that’s why I’ve now got a wheelchair which I use if I have to go out.
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: Imagine you get ten spoons of energy for the entire day – one to get out of bed, three for work, four for children. If you have ME, may take five spoons just to get out of bed and brush your teeth.
ME became known from the 1980s as yuppie flu and has had a bad reputation for being all in the head. Many still doubt it’s real but the World Health Organisation says over 17-million people from any age and race have it. 90% of those with ME are undiagnosed. Around five to 10% are said to recover.
NATHALIE WILLIAMS: Suicide is the leading cause of death among people with ME and I can totally understand that. Will they find a cure? Will I get better? Will I get worse? Those are the questions I try not to ask.
In San Francisco, California lives a family whose ME story has become a global rallying point for one of the biggest ever drives to find the cause and the cure. Thirty five year old Whitney Dafoe is a photographer and world traveller, but by 2013 it hurt too much to speak. Only his parents now enter his room but if they touch or talk to him, he’ll crash. His father is Dr Ron Davis.
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: How long did it take before your son was diagnosed with ME?
DR RON DAVIS, STANFORD MEDICINE & OPEN MEDICINE FOUNDATION: It took a few years. He went to...I do not know, 20, 30 doctors. All of them said there is nothing wrong with you. It is all in your head.
Coincidentally, Ron Davis is a celebrated geneticist and professor of biochemistry at Stanford University who’s been called one of the world’s greatest living inventors. His biotech methods helped launch the field of genome mapping. But now he’s changed professional gears, racing to find a cure in time to help his son.
DR RON DAVIS: The difficulty with the disease is if you do sort of standard medical tests and you look for liver function and kidney function and so forth, the patients look pretty normal. Although they don’t…they can’t do very much. And it is only when you use sort of the latest technologies...the high throughput sequencing, the gene expression studies...I mean you do that, you see oh my gosh, these people are very seriously ill.
The lack of a defining biomarker and treatments have caused doctors to dismiss it as psychosomatic. Supplements that help some are not covered by medical aid.
And then in 2011 the multi-million-pound UK PACE trial, announced in the respected Lancet Journal that exercise and psychotherapy were best for treating ME.
UC Berkeley's joint public health and journalism coordinator Dr David Tuller investigated claims that you just have to go for a walk and think happy thoughts.
DR DAVID TULLER, UC BERKELEY PUBLIC HEALTH & JOURNALISM: There is many, many flaws in the study and the patients had really pointed them all out before I started looking at it.
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: When the results were published, what kind of impact did it have?
DR DAVID TULLER: Well it had a pretty big impact because these are very well known psychiatrists; psychologists. They had been basically promoting these two therapies for many years before they actually did the trial.
Late last year, the PACE trial researchers were compelled to release their raw data after an Australian ME patient had submitted a Freedom of Information request in Britain. Turns out the study had included fatigued people who may not have had the full extent of ME.
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: What did the publishing of those results do to a now already confused landscape?
DR DAVID TULLER: They perpetuated a real misunderstanding around the world about what the illness is. That it is a physiological disease. It is not about: 'I do not feel like getting out of bed today'. It is like: 'I physically cannot move my body to get out of bed today, because I made myself a cup of coffee yesterday.'
DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: As debilitating and isolating as ME is, the internet has become a connector, linking those living with the disease.
Patients and PACE trial researchers continue to cross swords, but the researchers defend their work and are expanding their inquiry into online psycho-therapy in adolescents with ME.
The patient community staged an on- and offline revolt as the PACE message took root in treatment guidelines around the world. Demanding funding for research, they organised global protests for everyone who’s been missing from life due to ME.
PROTESTOR: My brother is severely ill - everyday he lies in bed fighting to stay alive, while waiting for death.
PROTESTOR: She got symptoms in her 20s - she’s now been in bed seven years.
PROTESTOR: It’s so hard to stand by and see our loved ones suffer.
PORTESTOR: We need the government to get involved and give us the funding that we need so that we can come up with a cure.
NATHALIE WILLIAMS: They spend more money in the States on researching male pattern baldness than they do on ME and this is a disease that can be fatal.
Nathalie’s joined an online support group that was started by Joburg-based Retha Viviers. The expanding group is a safe place to share baffling symptoms.
RETHA VIVIERS, ME/CFS FOUNDATION SOUTH AFRICA: It’s a lonely illness. I mean, I speak to my dogs, that’s my company. Comparing ME tiredness with normal healthy people’s tiredness is like comparing a match to an atom bomb. There is no comparison. You will have flu symptoms, throat will be sore, your body will ache, your brain will be completely dead.
A business graduate, Retha spends her few spoons of energy, in between sleeping, to source credible information and funds to help patients made destitute by ME.
RETHA VIVIERS: It’s like a cell phone battery that’s defective and you have to recharge it very often and you can’t use it while it’s being charged. So then I can function again for two, three hours, rest again and so my day goes. You know, you run out of funds, because you had to stop…I had to stop working and then I had to stop treatment.
Retha is fighting to break the stigma she faced when she lost everything. She’s inviting doctors to engage with the Foundation she’s started to learn about the latest science and inviting the public to get involved with funding.
RETHA VIVIERS: It would be very sad for people to commit suicide now or to lose hope now, because never before has there been so much hope. Professor Ron Davis says that they have done more in one year than the past thirty years. The other hope for South Africa in my humble view is the Foundation, because I believe we can change so many lives, getting funds, getting people diagnosed, getting symptomatic treatment to them, forming a community, getting care facilities in place. So people mustn’t lose hope now.
Symptoms that may signal ME include prolonged unrefreshing sleep; post-exertional malaise; cognitive impairment - literally losing words or numbers; insomnia; muscle and joint pain; frequent headaches; sore throat and lymph nodes; and intolerance to being upright, to light, sound, touch and chemicals.
RON DAVIS: There is a metabolic switch that happens when you are under extreme stress and that can be any type of stress...like auto accidents, surgery, an infection...that causes your body to sort of hunker down and shut down. It’s probably somewhat related to how animals can hibernate.
Davis has teamed up with a group including three Nobel laureates to raise funds to fast track the search for a cure. Open Medicine Foundation CEO Linda Tannenbaum’s daughter has ME - for her the collaboration of scientists that usually work for their own career advancement, is the gamechanger.
LINDA TANNENBAUM, CEO, OPEN MEDICINE FOUNDATION: Typically we wait for a paper to be published and then whoever sees it sees it. Instead we are going to have meetings and talk about what we are doing and put our results upon our website and you encourage people all over the world to look at the results...that is really the top reason that Open Medicine has a lot of hope for people.
RON DAVIS: We will find a biomarker, I am pretty convinced. A lot of people are looking for it.
DEVI: But unlike other researchers, your son is a daily reminder of why we need to move faster with the research.
RON DAVIS: And also why you worry about everyday, what have you done today to make it get us closer.

Carte Blanche looks into Chronic Fatigue – also known as Myalgic Encephalomyelitis. PROMOS: 15” How close is the breakthrough? We meet the scientists in a race against time to find a cure for crippling chronic fatigue syndrome. RETHA VIVIERS: ...never before has there been so much hope...they have done more in one year than the past 30 years. 15” NATHALIE WILLIAMS: They spend more money in the States on researching male pattern baldness than they do on ME and this is a disease that can be fatal. Chronic Fatigue Syndrome patients stands up to demand better research -- but will the cure come in time? 10” Lives lost to crippling chronic fatigue syndrome fight for research and recognition -- how long before science reveals the solutions that up to 20-million people are desperate for? Script: SCRIPT: MILLIONS MISSING TX: 12 February 2017 PRODUCER: Anna-Maria van Niekerk INSERT SCRIPT NATHALIE WILLIAMS: I wake up every day of the life and it doesn’t matter how many hours I have slept. I still feel tired. In Fourways Johannesburg, Nathalie Williams has moved back into her mom’s home. She’d love nothing better than to get out and go to work. Or take her dogs for a walk. But in the 26th year of living with myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome, she can’t. NATHALIE WILLIAMS: I hate the term chronic fatigue syndrome...first of all, fatigue is...that doesn’t even come close to describing what it is and second of all, it’s...it’s a minor symptom really compared to the other stuff. Nathalie would pay a high price for pushing through with this hour-long interview – they call it the push-crash cycle – crippling pain, debilitating brain fog – in ME it’s called post-exertional malaise. Like the worst influenza, it kicks in after a day or so – for some triggered by lifting the sheets on their bed – for Nathalie, being upright. NATHALIE WILLIAMS: Anytime you’re upright, your heart has to pump more blood around the body and with people with ME, our hearts don’t pump blood properly...I start to sweat, I feel dizzy and I feel nauseous, that’s why I’ve now got a wheelchair which I use if I have to go out. DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: Imagine you get ten spoons of energy for the entire day – one to get out of bed, three for work, four for children. If you have ME, may take five spoons just to get out of bed and brush your teeth. ME became known from the 1980s as yuppie flu and has had a bad reputation for being all in the head. Many still doubt it’s real but the World Health Organisation says over 17-million people from any age and race have it. 90% of those with ME are undiagnosed. Around five to 10% are said to recover. NATHALIE WILLIAMS: Suicide is the leading cause of death among people with ME and I can totally understand that. Will they find a cure? Will I get better? Will I get worse? Those are the questions I try not to ask. In San Francisco, California lives a family whose ME story has become a global rallying point for one of the biggest ever drives to find the cause and the cure. Thirty five year old Whitney Dafoe is a photographer and world traveller, but by 2013 it hurt too much to speak. Only his parents now enter his room but if they touch or talk to him, he’ll crash. His father is Dr Ron Davis. DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: How long did it take before your son was diagnosed with ME? DR RON DAVIS, STANFORD MEDICINE & OPEN MEDICINE FOUNDATION: It took a few years. He went to...I do not know, 20, 30 doctors. All of them said there is nothing wrong with you. It is all in your head. Coincidentally, Ron Davis is a celebrated geneticist and professor of biochemistry at Stanford University who’s been called one of the world’s greatest living inventors. His biotech methods helped launch the field of genome mapping. But now he’s changed professional gears, racing to find a cure in time to help his son. DR RON DAVIS: The difficulty with the disease is if you do sort of standard medical tests and you look for liver function and kidney function and so forth, the patients look pretty normal. Although they don’t…they can’t do very much. And it is only when you use sort of the latest technologies...the high throughput sequencing, the gene expression studies...I mean you do that, you see oh my gosh, these people are very seriously ill. The lack of a defining biomarker and treatments have caused doctors to dismiss it as psychosomatic. Supplements that help some are not covered by medical aid. And then in 2011 the multi-million-pound UK PACE trial, announced in the respected Lancet Journal that exercise and psychotherapy were best for treating ME. UC Berkeley's joint public health and journalism coordinator Dr David Tuller investigated claims that you just have to go for a walk and think happy thoughts. DR DAVID TULLER, UC BERKELEY PUBLIC HEALTH & JOURNALISM: There is many, many flaws in the study and the patients had really pointed them all out before I started looking at it. DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: When the results were published, what kind of impact did it have? DR DAVID TULLER: Well it had a pretty big impact because these are very well known psychiatrists; psychologists. They had been basically promoting these two therapies for many years before they actually did the trial. Late last year, the PACE trial researchers were compelled to release their raw data after an Australian ME patient had submitted a Freedom of Information request in Britain. Turns out the study had included fatigued people who may not have had the full extent of ME. DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: What did the publishing of those results do to a now already confused landscape? DR DAVID TULLER: They perpetuated a real misunderstanding around the world about what the illness is. That it is a physiological disease. It is not about: 'I do not feel like getting out of bed today'. It is like: 'I physically cannot move my body to get out of bed today, because I made myself a cup of coffee yesterday.' DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: As debilitating and isolating as ME is, the internet has become a connector, linking those living with the disease. Patients and PACE trial researchers continue to cross swords, but the researchers defend their work and are expanding their inquiry into online psycho-therapy in adolescents with ME. The patient community staged an on- and offline revolt as the PACE message took root in treatment guidelines around the world. Demanding funding for research, they organised global protests for everyone who’s been missing from life due to ME. PROTESTOR: My brother is severely ill - everyday he lies in bed fighting to stay alive, while waiting for death. PROTESTOR: She got symptoms in her 20s - she’s now been in bed seven years. PROTESTOR: It’s so hard to stand by and see our loved ones suffer. PORTESTOR: We need the government to get involved and give us the funding that we need so that we can come up with a cure. NATHALIE WILLIAMS: They spend more money in the States on researching male pattern baldness than they do on ME and this is a disease that can be fatal. Nathalie’s joined an online support group that was started by Joburg-based Retha Viviers. The expanding group is a safe place to share baffling symptoms. RETHA VIVIERS, ME/CFS FOUNDATION SOUTH AFRICA: It’s a lonely illness. I mean, I speak to my dogs, that’s my company. Comparing ME tiredness with normal healthy people’s tiredness is like comparing a match to an atom bomb. There is no comparison. You will have flu symptoms, throat will be sore, your body will ache, your brain will be completely dead. A business graduate, Retha spends her few spoons of energy, in between sleeping, to source credible information and funds to help patients made destitute by ME. RETHA VIVIERS: It’s like a cell phone battery that’s defective and you have to recharge it very often and you can’t use it while it’s being charged. So then I can function again for two, three hours, rest again and so my day goes. You know, you run out of funds, because you had to stop…I had to stop working and then I had to stop treatment. Retha is fighting to break the stigma she faced when she lost everything. She’s inviting doctors to engage with the Foundation she’s started to learn about the latest science and inviting the public to get involved with funding. RETHA VIVIERS: It would be very sad for people to commit suicide now or to lose hope now, because never before has there been so much hope. Professor Ron Davis says that they have done more in one year than the past thirty years. The other hope for South Africa in my humble view is the Foundation, because I believe we can change so many lives, getting funds, getting people diagnosed, getting symptomatic treatment to them, forming a community, getting care facilities in place. So people mustn’t lose hope now. Symptoms that may signal ME include prolonged unrefreshing sleep; post-exertional malaise; cognitive impairment - literally losing words or numbers; insomnia; muscle and joint pain; frequent headaches; sore throat and lymph nodes; and intolerance to being upright, to light, sound, touch and chemicals. RON DAVIS: There is a metabolic switch that happens when you are under extreme stress and that can be any type of stress...like auto accidents, surgery, an infection...that causes your body to sort of hunker down and shut down. It’s probably somewhat related to how animals can hibernate. Davis has teamed up with a group including three Nobel laureates to raise funds to fast track the search for a cure. Open Medicine Foundation CEO Linda Tannenbaum’s daughter has ME - for her the collaboration of scientists that usually work for their own career advancement, is the gamechanger. LINDA TANNENBAUM, CEO, OPEN MEDICINE FOUNDATION: Typically we wait for a paper to be published and then whoever sees it sees it. Instead we are going to have meetings and talk about what we are doing and put our results upon our website and you encourage people all over the world to look at the results...that is really the top reason that Open Medicine has a lot of hope for people. RON DAVIS: We will find a biomarker, I am pretty convinced. A lot of people are looking for it. DEVI: But unlike other researchers, your son is a daily reminder of why we need to move faster with the research. RON DAVIS: And also why you worry about everyday, what have you done today to make it get us closer.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Twenty to 30-million people worldwide have dropped out of life due to a mysterious illness that can't be cured, nor its origins traced. But is there finally hope after years of misdiagnosis?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Millions of very ill people are wrestling their lives back from misunderstanding and stigmatization around a crippling disease called myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) or chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). There’s no known cure for CFS and the origins are still poorly understood – to make matters worse, bad science that led to totally inappropriate understanding and treatment of the disease in the last five years very nearly became a prolonged death sentence for the millions of people living with CFS.
metadata.Summary: CFS has been called a malingerer’s disease - it occurs in people of all ages, socio-economic levels and ethnic backgrounds, even toddlers as young as 2. Many doctors remain unconvinced of CFS as a genuine illness; no cause or diagnostic test exist. Much damage was done to the CFS cause when in 2011 British researchers announced a major breakthrough in the highly respected journal Lancet. The researchers reported that ‘PACE’, the largest treatment trial ever had been a great success and "found" that the best way of dealing with CFS was exercise and psychotherapy. Graded exercise therapy (GET) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) would improve the symptoms and could even cure CFS. CBT would challenge patients’ beliefs that they have a physiological illness limiting their ability to exercise and so they need only to become more active and ignore their symptoms to fully recover. Headlines around the world shouted, “Got ME? Just get out and exercise, say scientists.” The medical profession, including American CDC, soon set PACE as baseline for treatment guidelines. Problem is, PACE was bad science. CFS sufferers realised it straight away. Science is only now catching up with exactly how bad. PACE contradicted patients' everyday experience that even mild exertion could increase all other symptoms and cause fatigue so profound that they could barely lift the sheets on their beds. It caused cognitive deficits, blood pressure problems, unrestorative sleep, neurological and immune dysfunction, among about 60 symptoms. At first, the "Missing Millions" had no way of challenging the science, because the data of the study hadn’t been released, but what they COULD do was send emails, chat online…and form a community that began to fight back against their physical and conceptual imprisonment. A five-year battle ensued to review the actual data underlying the $8-million PACE study.
metadata.Further information: In the last two months, in September, the Missing Millions made a great breakthrough when a British court ordered the PACE trial's original data to be released. Rewind a few years - in South Africa, Retha Viviers had founded a Facebook support group that is growing at a steady pace and it encouraged her to begin the ME/CFS Foundation South Africa to focus on awareness, diagnosis, and treatment of the disease. Retha hooked up with the US-based Open Medicine Foundation of Dr Ronald Davis to bring home messages of hope; get financial support for bed-ridden breadwinners who have lost everything…and this Retha has done mostly from her own bed, as CFS forces her to economise every movement of her life. In stark contrast to a silent, isolated world before social media, CFS patients were now able to start identifying patterns and shared experiences. They began to realise it’s not all in their heads and that most of them really do have to REST the minute they feel tired, not exercise...otherwise the next day they’d be semi-paralyzed, barely able to walk. Many patients worked to bring the flaws of the PACE study to light. They wrote blogs, contacted the press, submitted carefully argued letters and commentaries to leading medical journals. They even published papers in peer-reviewed scientific journals. Patients organised to file Freedom of Information Act requests to gain access to the trial data from Queen Mary University of London where the lead researcher worked. The university denied most of the requests, saying they were “vexatious.” The study’s defenders painted critics as unhinged crusaders who were “impeding progress for the estimated 30-million ME/CFS patients around the world”. Richard Horton, the editor of the Lancet described the trial’s critics as “a fairly small but highly organised, very vocal and very damaging group of individuals who have, I would say, actually hijacked this agenda and distorted the debate so that it actually harms the overwhelming majority of patients.” Press reports alleged that ME/CFS researchers had received death threats, and they lumped the PACE critics in with the purported crazies. But the online community of “activists” managed under court order to compel the British researchers to release their raw data which they did this past September. PACE had seemed like a great study — big, controlled, peer-reviewed — but patients couldn’t reconcile the results with their own experience so as the dug into the data the saw enormous problems became clear and once they’d done their analyses, the investigation was taken forward by Dr. David Tuller, a lecturer in public health and journalism at UC Berkeley. The collective effort helped demolish the credibility of the PACE trial as a piece of scientific research. In February this year Virology Blog posted an open letter to The Lancet and its editor, Richard Horton, stating that the trial’s flaws “have no place in published research.” Surprisingly, the PACE authors, The Lancet, and others in the U.K. medical and academic establishment have continued their vigorous defense of the study, despite its glaring methodological and ethical deficiencies. The analysis shows that if you’re already getting standard medical care, your chances of being helped by exercise and psychotherapy are at best 10% and chances of recovery nearly 0%. Under the guidance of world-renowned geneticist Ronald W. Davis, PhD, Open Medicine Foundation has brought in top experts from a variety of fields for a bold and new collaborative research project with the ultimate goal of unlocking the mystery ME/CFS. Davis’ own son, the 30-year old Whitney, suffers from CFS and Davis is determined to find a cure – even if it might be too late for his own son, who is reportedly terminally ill. Davis' "End ME/CFS Project" was founded on the idea that a comprehensive, interdisciplinary effort is needed to produce breakthroughs in the understanding of ME/CFS and related chronic complex diseases (sometimes referred to as neuro-immune diseases). Their goal is to connect the best experts, from both inside and outside the field, through openness and information sharing. Linda Tannenbaum, Open Medicine Foundation’s CEO/President also has a personal motivation for wanting to find answers as quickly as possible, because has a daughter suffering from ME/CFS. The project’s first study is the ME/CFS Severely ill Big Data Study that is designed to find a clinically useful diagnostic biomarker. “Almost all scientists do things that are easy,” said Dr. Davis. “That’s why no one has done this study before.” Davis calls the PACE research a “classic bad study” that used such a broad definition of the disease that it likely included many patients who didn’t truly have ME/CFS at all. Davis says the PACE study has to be retracted or even used as a teaching tool to have medical students identify how many things are wrong the study. Retractions are rare, however, and erasing the impact of this flawed research will take much work for years to come. Davis expects his project to succeed because it’s modeled after two former success stories – the The Human Genome Project, launched by James D. Watson, PhD, who is on our ME/CFS Scientific Advisory Board and the Consortium on Inflammation and Host Response to Injury in Humans, led by Ronald G. Tompkins, also on the ME/CFS Scientific Advisory Board. For the first time, high level scientists are working on increasing understanding of the disease at a molecular level and find diagnostic markers, effective treatments, and a cure. They also hope to fine effective prevention strategies.
